questions.q: Which of the following qualifies as a "secret" in a DevSecOps context?
options: Only values explicitly labeled "password" in a form
Any value whose disclosure would let someone impersonate a service, access protected data, or cause financial harm
Only credentials used in production environments
Only values longer than 20 characters
questions.explain: Secrets include connection strings, API keys, TLS/SSH keys, signing keys, and webhook secrets — anything whose disclosure causes real harm, not just values literally named "password".

questions.q: Why doesn't deleting a hardcoded secret in a later git commit actually remove the risk?
options: Git automatically re-adds deleted lines after 30 days
The secret is still recoverable from git history unless history is rewritten and the credential is rotated
Deleting a line in git immediately purges it from every clone
It does fully remove the risk, no further action needed
questions.explain: Git history retains prior commits, so a secret committed once remains recoverable from history even after a later commit removes the line — rotation and history rewriting are needed to actually close the exposure.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is "just don't commit secrets" an insufficient policy on its own?
options: Because developers are generally careless and can't be trusted
Because the causes are structural — local dev needs some credential source, verbose logging is a common default, and incident-response pressure favors fast but insecure sharing
Because git itself prevents all secret commits automatically
Because secrets never actually leak in well-run organizations
questions.explain: The lesson argues the real causes are structural, not a discipline failure — which is why making the secure path the easy path (vaults, automated scanning) matters more than reminders alone.

questions.q: What happened in Northbridge Retail's real incident described in this lesson?
options: A production database password was posted publicly on social media
A sandbox API key was committed via a .env.local file missing from .gitignore, and was caught three weeks later by a secrets-detection scan
An attacker brute-forced an admin password
A customer's credit card number was logged in plaintext
questions.explain: The incident involved a sandbox credential committed through a missing .gitignore, caught by an automated scan after three weeks — limited impact, but it prompted a vault-first policy going forward.

questions.q: Why is logging an application's full configuration at startup a common leak pattern?
options: Logs are never stored anywhere after being written
Logging systems often have broader read access than the secret itself should have, exposing it to more people than intended
Logging frameworks automatically encrypt all secret values
This pattern is not actually a real risk in practice
questions.explain: A centralized logging system frequently has a wider audience of readers than the original secret was meant to have, so a plaintext secret in a startup log ends up more exposed than the developer intended.
